title: Sweet Sixteen

jokes.text: Oh, Ann, you beautiful, rule-breaking moth.
jokes.setup: Ann asks Leslie to approve her campaign poster, a simple yes/no request.
jokes.punchline: Leslie greets Ann with an absurdly florid, slightly wrong compliment — 'moth' instead of something conventionally flattering.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's bizarre Ann-compliments are a series hallmark, and 'moth' is a perfect specimen — it sounds complimentary, rhymes with the butterfly pattern, but is objectively unflattering. The specificity ('rule-breaking') and the wrongness of 'moth' make it land well. High character integration because this is essentially Leslie's love language rendered absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Do you want the campaign posters to say 'Vote Leslie Knope' or 'Leslie Knope for City Council'?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, those posters aren't just about words on paper. They're a clarion call to the citizens of Pawnee, a rallying cry that echoes through the streets like a majestic eagle soaring over the Grand Canyon at sunset, reminding every man, woman, and child that there is hope, there is possibility, and there is Leslie Knope.

jokes.text: Boss, I need your Herbie Hancock on this.
jokes.setup: Ben needs a signature on a document.
jokes.punchline: He says 'Herbie Hancock' instead of 'John Hancock,' a malapropism that conflates the Founding Father with the jazz musician.
jokes.explanation: A reasonably witty wordplay moment. The confusion of John Hancock with Herbie Hancock is a small, enjoyable gag with decent economy. Not especially character-specific — almost anyone could say this — but it earns a mild chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I need you to Herbie Hancock this for me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Outside.

jokes.text: Leslie abruptly steps outside the government building to say 'Yes' to Ann's question, then steps back in.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains she cannot do campaign business inside the government building.
jokes.punchline: She steps outside, says one word ('Outside.'), then walks back in — the rule followed to a comic extreme.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag inferred from context — Leslie steps outside to say a single word then re-enters. It's a perfectly Leslie move: rigid rule-following taken to absurd but logical extremes. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, the campaign finance rules are actually a great opportunity for us to focus on grassroots organizing and authentic community engagement instead of spending money on ads and—you know what? This is insane. We're going to lose. We're going to lose so badly.

jokes.text: April suggests making the rule-following 'more fun' and produces something (implied comically over-the-top) to Leslie's exasperated reaction.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to make the campaign/work separation feel like 'a fun game.'
jokes.punchline: April immediately finds a way to one-up her framing with something absurd, cut before the reveal, leaving Leslie horrified.
jokes.explanation: The cut before the reveal is a reliable Parks trick. April's mischief is well-characterized and the setup earns the reaction, but it's mild without knowing what she produced. Comedy of implication.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay April, this is going to be so fun! We're going to play a game where you follow these rules. Rule one: you have to smile. Rule two: you have to say nice things. Rule three: you have to participate in team building activities.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not a game, that's just... your life.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no! It IS a game because I made up rules! See? Rule four: if you break any of the other rules, you have to do the rules again, but this time while thinking about how fun it is!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're describing a psychological nightmare.

jokes.text: I'm pretty sure you've worn that sweater four days in a row. / Or I own four identical versions of the same sweater. / No, you don't, there's an old lollipop that's been stuck to the back since Tuesday.
jokes.setup: Ron is making the case that Leslie is exhausted and overextended, citing the sweater as evidence.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's denial is reasonable on its face ('four identical sweaters' is plausible for her), then Ron immediately demolishes it with the lollipop detail — specific, disgusting, and irrefutable.
jokes.explanation: A three-beat joke with excellent structure: accusation → plausible denial → devastating specificity. 'Since Tuesday' lands the kicker. The lollipop is funny on its own as a physical detail, but the fact that it makes Leslie's denial totally untenable makes it great. High character integration: Ron's deadpan precision and Leslie's exhausted spin are both perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh wow, a game about municipal government? That sounds absolutely thrilling. I can't wait to spend my evening learning about zoning permits and budget allocations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right? I know, it's so much fun!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gonna go ahead and hang up now.

jokes.text: That's the style now, Ron. It's called 'lollipopping.' All the kids are doing it.
jokes.setup: Ron has just proven Leslie wore the same sweater for four days via a lollipop stuck to the back.
jokes.punchline: Leslie doubles down and invents a trend name for her embarrassing situation with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: The immediate pivot to 'lollipopping' as a named trend is a great Leslie move — she is constitutionally incapable of admitting defeat and will construct an alternate reality rather than concede. 'All the kids are doing it' is the topper. The word 'lollipopping' itself is funny. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're overworked. You need to delegate more.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're right, Ron. So I'm starting a new department: The Department of Delegation Oversight and Management. D.D.O.M. We'll meet every morning at 6 AM to discuss delegation strategies.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's the opposite of what I said.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know! Isn't it great?

jokes.text: Leslie accepts Ron's 'apology' he never gave and announces they've reached the 'agreement' that she won't take a sabbatical.
jokes.setup: Ron firmly tells Leslie she needs to take a sabbatical.
jokes.punchline: Leslie thanks him for his 'apology' and announces their 'agreement' that she won't take one — inverting the entire conversation.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's complete reframing of a conversation she clearly lost is a sharp character joke. Her insistence on her own narrative reality over literal events is well-established and executed crisply here. Ron's silence in response is also funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not the same sweater! I have several identical sweaters.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: There's a Cheeto dust stain in the exact same spot on the shoulder. You've worn the same sweater four days in a row.

jokes.text: Nobody owns me, cupcake, not even you. You can either burn these hats in a fire, or you can use a blowtorch.
jokes.setup: Ann objects to being labeled 'Tommy's Girl' with no reciprocal ownership acknowledged.
jokes.punchline: Tom insists on his freedom while simultaneously offering only two destruction options for the hats — both fire-based — as if those are the only choices.
jokes.explanation: The two fire options (fire or blowtorch — same thing) is a small absurdist gem. Tom's pseudo-philosophical 'nobody owns me' stance undercut by his petty hat design is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, it's not dirty, it's vintage. And these aren't stains, they're... they're artisanal candy accents. Very European. Very now.

jokes.text: How about this option? We put the hats on-- / Don't say it. / We take everything else off.
jokes.setup: Ann is about to reject another hat-related option Tom is proposing.
jokes.punchline: Tom's option is to wear only the hats — Ann correctly anticipated the direction and tried to stop it; Tom delivers it anyway.
jokes.explanation: The 'don't say it' / says it anyway beat is a well-worn sitcom structure. Ann's anticipation adds a layer, but the joke itself is fairly predictable. Mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I think you should take a sabbatical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Ron, I appreciate you saying that. And I'm glad we both agree that I'm indispensable to this office. Thank you for the apology.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I didn't apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, Ron, Ron. We've both said some things. The important thing is we've worked through it and we're moving forward together.

jokes.text: These Kangol hats are exactly like the one Samuel L. Jackson wore to the Latin Grammys. How could she not like them?
jokes.setup: Tom is baffled by Ann's rejection of his hat gift.
jokes.punchline: His defense invokes a very specific — and odd — cultural reference: Samuel L. Jackson at the Latin Grammys. The specificity of the event makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Tom treating Samuel L. Jackson at the Latin Grammys as an incontrovertible fashion authority is very in-character. The specificity of 'Latin Grammys' elevates what could be a basic name-drop into something more absurd and funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I got this gift for the most beautiful girl in Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, that's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait... you're standing right here.

jokes.text: I kind of set up Tom and Ann, and now they won't stop asking me for advice, which is a really bad move on their part, because I really don't care what happens to them... Or anyone.
jokes.setup: April gives a talking-head explaining her position on being Tom and Ann's advisor.
jokes.punchline: The escalating disavowal ending with '...Or anyone' — a beat that reframes her indifference as cosmic.
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Or anyone' is the entire joke and it lands because April's nihilism is so consistent and genuine. High character integration — this is the most April sentence possible. The economy is good; she doesn't belabor it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, why do we have to wear matching hats? That's so gendered.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, cupcake, I'm declaring my independence from hat-based gender norms.

jokes.text: As the Germans would say, 'er ist ein wunder hund.' He is a wonder dog.
jokes.setup: Chris returns Champion the dog after dogsitting overnight.
jokes.punchline: Chris casually drops German and then immediately translates it himself, revealing he learned dog-specific German only — not actual fluency.
jokes.explanation: The joke builds nicely: Chris shows off German, self-translates (mild deflation), then the talking-head reveals his German is exclusively dog-related. That final specification is the best part. Very Chris — overachieving in a completely pointless domain.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, whatever you're about to say, don't.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I was just gonna say we should have intercourse.

jokes.text: The dog training course I took was conducted entirely in German, and so now I'm fluent in German... Words relating to dogs.
jokes.setup: Chris claimed to be 'fluent in German' in the previous beat.
jokes.punchline: Talking-head clarification: his German is limited exclusively to dog-training vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff that makes the prior moment great. 'Fluent in German... Words relating to dogs' is perfectly structured — the ellipsis before the qualifier does the comedic work. Chris's absurd overachievement in narrow domains is a great character trait, and this is one of its funniest expressions. The economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann doesn't like the hats? But I specifically designed them to be cool. They're like what Samuel L. Jackson would wear to the Latin Grammys if he went to the Latin Grammys, which he won't, because he's not Latin.

jokes.text: He's a mutt. Half amazing, half terrific.
jokes.setup: Chris describes Champion as a wonderful dog.
jokes.punchline: Andy describes the dog's mixed breed as 'half amazing, half terrific' — two synonyms treated as distinct breeds.
jokes.explanation: Possibly the tightest, best-constructed joke in the episode. Andy sincerely uses two synonyms as if they're meaningful genetic distinctions. It's deeply Andy — wholehearted, earnest, and completely wrong in the most endearing way. The economy is exceptional: six words, perfectly weighted. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not good at giving relationship advice because I don't actually care about anyone.

jokes.text: Ich bin ein three-legged dog.
jokes.setup: Chris has been showing off his dog-German vocabulary.
jokes.punchline: He riffs on JFK's 'Ich bin ein Berliner' by substituting 'three-legged dog' — simultaneously a grammar demonstration and a non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: A clever little JFK reference riff that earns a smile from the absurdity of the combination. Not a huge laugh but a witty grace note. The joke works better for viewers who catch the allusion.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: His name is Champion. He's a very good boy. Sehr guter Junge.

jokes.text: Wait, did his leg grow back?
jokes.setup: Chris says Champion is 'healthier than ever' after his week of care.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately wonders if 'healthier than ever' means a new leg grew — sincere, hopeful, and completely impossible.
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly capture Andy's childlike magical thinking. The hope in the question is what makes it funny — he genuinely wonders. It's an absurdist non sequitur grounded in total character authenticity. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm fluent in German.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Really? Say something in German.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Uh... Die Bratwurst ist sehr lecker.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's just about sausage.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yes. I am fluent in German sausage.

jokes.text: Dogs tend to take on the personalities of their owners — so if you were to sit on your couch all day watching cartoons and eating nothing but Cheetos, that's what he would want to do too. / Who wouldn't? That sounds like an amazing day, right?
jokes.setup: Chris uses the personality-mirroring fact to gently suggest Andy should be more active for Champion's sake.
jokes.punchline: Andy completely misses the implicit criticism and endorses the couch/Cheetos lifestyle as aspirational.
jokes.explanation: Andy's obliviousness to the implied criticism and his genuine enthusiasm for the Cheeto lifestyle is a reliable Andy move executed well. Chris's earnest parenting-style delivery makes the contrast funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Champion is a mixed breed. A lot of people might call him a mutt, but I prefer to think of him as a dog with a very diverse genetic portfolio. He's got a little bit of everything - German Shepherd, Labrador, some Collie maybe. It's like he's a living metaphor for the beautiful diversity of the canine world.

jokes.text: Jerry, take that shirt off. You look ridiculous.
jokes.setup: Jerry shows up wearing a new birthday shirt from his wife.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate, harsh command (without even knowing it's a birthday gift) sets up the Jerry-humiliation-that-turns-emotional arc.
jokes.explanation: Functions more as a plot beat than a pure joke, but there's comedic value in Leslie's reflexive Jerry-criticism. Mild laugh, mostly setup for the birthday revelation that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been studying German, and I want to impress you with my knowledge of dog-related vocabulary.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: The German word for dog is 'hund.' A puppy is 'welpe.' And a really good boy is 'sehr guter hund.'

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: But here's where it gets interesting. If you combine the words, you get 'hundewelpeseHrguterhund,' which is technically one word in German.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It means 'a dog puppy that is very good and also respects fitness routines and has perfect posture.'

jokes.text: Jerry reveals his birthday is February 29th — he only gets a real birthday every four years.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Jerry to take his birthday shirt off because he looks ridiculous.
jokes.punchline: It's revealed Jerry has a leap-day birthday — a genuinely unfortunate fact that adds to his cosmic bad luck.
jokes.explanation: The leap-day birthday is a perfect Jerry detail — universally relatable bad luck amplified to absurdity. It also enables the entire episode premise. Good character integration because it fits the 'Jerry can't win' mythology of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You just sit around all day doing nothing, eating terrible food, not exercising, completely disregarding your health and responsibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know! Isn't it great?

jokes.text: I'm so sorry we forgot yours. I guess it just slipped through the cracks. / Yes, I guess it did.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been telling Ron that things are NOT slipping through the cracks.
jokes.punchline: She uses the exact phrase 'slipped through the cracks' about Jerry's birthday — immediately after Ron used it to describe her failures. Jerry's quiet, gentle agreement makes it land.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Ron's exact phrasing is elegant and self-aware. Jerry's quiet 'Yes, I guess it did' is the perfect response — not bitter, just accurate. Good structural irony.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My birthday is February 29th. I was born on leap day.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So technically, I've only had twelve real birthdays.

jokes.text: Also I need you to do some fecal contamination testing at the reservoir. / Now? / Yes, go get a kit from maintenance, and I need you to check the water for bird dung.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just sincerely apologized to Jerry for forgetting his birthday.
jokes.punchline: In the same breath, she sends him to test water for bird poop — on his birthday, immediately after the emotional moment.
jokes.explanation: The abrupt pivot from warm apology to bird-poop-testing duty is a reliable Parks gag. The specificity of 'bird dung' is a small upgrade over 'contamination.' Jerry's plaintive 'Can I at least grab the gloves?' adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I went to this place called Cakey J's Cheesecake Facility for my birthday.

jokes.text: Jerry, what are you doing standing here? Our water has poop in it.
jokes.setup: Jerry pauses, presumably to process the birthday-then-poop-duty whiplash.
jokes.punchline: Ron frames a municipal health crisis as a personal affront to Jerry's work ethic, using the word 'poop' with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: 'Our water has poop in it' is a beautifully blunt Ron Swanson line. His use of 'poop' rather than a more bureaucratic term, combined with his deadpan urgency, is pitch-perfect Ron. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: So I had the most incredible birthday celebration. We started by going skydiving, then we went to this exclusive nightclub where I danced until 3 AM, then we went to this five-star restaurant and had the most amazing meal of my life, and then... we went to bed early.

jokes.text: 64 divided by 4 is-- / 16. / 64. / So we're gonna throw him a Sweet 16 surprise party.
jokes.setup: The group is working out Jerry's 'real' age based on leap-year birthdays.
jokes.punchline: Someone correctly says '16,' someone incorrectly says '64,' and Leslie uses the concept to declare a Sweet 16 party — the math joke resolves into absurd party logic.
jokes.explanation: The math confusion (someone confuses 64 divided by 4 = 16 with the answer being 64 again) is a small but real laugh, especially followed by Leslie's enthusiastic leap to 'Sweet 16 party.' The absurdity of the concept lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So if Jerry was born on a leap day, he'd only have a birthday every four years. Let me think... if he's 61...

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's 15.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, April, that's not even close.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We should throw him a Sweet 16 party. With a limo and those sashes.

jokes.text: Four years from now, who knows? He might be retired... Or dead. / Let's start a pool. Who wants retired? Who wants dead? / Dead. / No.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining why Jerry's birthday is so important.
jokes.punchline: The group casually bets on whether Jerry will be retired or dead in four years, with Tom immediately voting 'dead.'
jokes.explanation: Dark but light-footed — the show's casual cruelty toward Jerry is funny precisely because it's so matter-of-fact. Tom's immediate 'Dead' vote and Ben's horrified 'No' capture the office dynamic. The 'let's start a pool' framing is a nice Leslie touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry might be retired or dead in four years.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm starting a betting pool on when Jerry dies.

jokes.text: Donna reveals her family has a lake house but keeps it quiet: 'We're not big on hospitality. The Meagles are a cold people.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if they can use Donna's lake house.
jokes.punchline: Donna explains the secrecy: her family keeps the house quiet because they're simply not warm people — delivered as a plain family fact.
jokes.explanation: 'The Meagles are a cold people' is a genuinely funny line — the use of the family surname with tribal gravitas ('a cold people') is an absurdist construction delivered with Donna's trademark flat authority. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Fine. You can use my lake house. But I'm warning you, my family is cold. Not emotionally—we're very warm. I mean literally cold. We don't believe in heating. It's a waste of money and it builds character.

jokes.text: Donna's lake house rules: no dirty shoes, upstairs is Meagle space only, and — pointedly — 'you do not have access to the hot tub.'
jokes.setup: The group arrives at Donna's beautiful lake house.
jokes.punchline: The house rules include a specific denial of hot tub access — delivered as the most important rule.
jokes.explanation: Donna's territorial protectiveness of her property and especially the hot tub is a great character beat. The escalation from 'no dirty shoes' (reasonable) to 'Meagle space only' (firm) to 'you do not have access to the hot tub' (emphatic) builds well.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: That's the sound of the ice maker. And that's the sound of me denying you access to it.

jokes.text: Ginuwine's my cousin. / Ginuwine? / The Ginuwine is your cousin? / How do I not know this? / Who's Ginuwine? / Ginuwine?
jokes.setup: The group spots a Ginuwine platinum record and photo with Donna at the lake house.
jokes.punchline: Donna casually reveals Ginuwine is her cousin — various characters react with awe (Ben, Tom), confusion (April), and a hilarious group cascade of saying his name.
jokes.explanation: The cascade of reactions to 'Ginuwine is my cousin' is executed well — each character's response is true to them (Tom's awe, April's cluelessness, Chris's ignorance). The name 'Ginuwine' itself is inherently funny to repeat, and the show leans into that with the group saying it multiple times.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, is that... Ginuwine memorabilia? Why do you have all this?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: He's my cousin.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your cousin? Ginuwine is your cousin?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Yeah. We don't really talk about it.

jokes.text: Ginuwine is Ginuwine. He's Ginuwine.
jokes.setup: Someone (likely April or Chris) doesn't know who Ginuwine is and keeps asking.
jokes.punchline: Tom's explanation of who Ginuwine is simply restates his name three times as if that's sufficient.
jokes.explanation: Tom's tautological 'explanation' — Ginuwine is Ginuwine, he's Ginuwine — is a perfectly stupid and perfectly constructed moment. It captures both Tom's reverence for the artist and his complete inability to articulate why. The triple repetition of the name earns big laughs because it reveals that Tom thinks the name alone should be enough. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ginuwine. The R&B singer. He's only one of the greatest artists of all time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know who that is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ginuwine. Ginuwine the Pony Boy. He sings 'Pony.' The song 'Pony.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Still not ringing a bell.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How do you not know Ginuwine?! Ginuwine! GI-NU-WINE!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is he a food?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No! He's Ginuwine! The artist! Ginuwine!

jokes.text: Saying his name over and over again is not going to help me.
jokes.setup: Tom has just explained Ginuwine by repeating his name three times.
jokes.punchline: April's flat observation that name-repetition isn't informative is delivered with perfect deadpan.
jokes.explanation: April's calm, accurate observation is the perfect deflation of Tom's enthusiasm. It's funny because she's completely right and Tom is completely wrong. April's deadpan suits it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I have some dealbreakers. You need to have seen all of The Wire. You need to understand the cultural significance of the original Ghostbusters. And you need to know that the second Die Hard movie isn't a Christmas movie.

jokes.text: Not loving '90s R&B music is number three on the 'oh-no-nos' list.
jokes.setup: Tom explains he has a list of relationship dealbreakers called 'oh-no-nos.'
jokes.punchline: Not loving '90s R&B is number three — implying there are at least two worse dealbreakers, and that this is a real, ranked list.
jokes.explanation: The concept of a ranked 'oh-no-nos' list is very Tom, and revealing it exists and has at least three entries (with Ginuwine-related music at #3) is funny. The audience naturally wonders what #1 and #2 are. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Merkel!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Did you just use the German Chancellor's name as a dog command?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, yes. In Germany, we use 'Merkel' to—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's incredible.

jokes.text: Girl doesn't even know who Ginuwine is.
jokes.setup: Ann has revealed she doesn't know who Ginuwine is.
jokes.punchline: Tom delivers this to the camera in genuine heartbreak — as if this is a serious character failing.
jokes.explanation: Tom's confessional devastation over Ann's Ginuwine ignorance is a good character beat — his sincerity about trivial things is always funny. But it's largely a repeat of the prior Ginuwine beats.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm multitasking like a boss! I can handle the budget report AND eat this sandwich at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: See? Nailed it. I'm basically a superhero.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you just dropped the entire sandwich on the budget report.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well... I guess I'm eating crow now. Literally, if this is what I think it is.

jokes.text: Leslie multitasks a phone interview while decorating for Jerry's party. Ron in a talking head: 'Crow for dinner tonight, Mr. Swanson?'
jokes.setup: Leslie claimed she could handle everything; Ron was skeptical. Now she's clearly managing at least two things at once.
jokes.punchline: Ron's talking head — 'Crow for dinner tonight, Mr. Swanson?' — acknowledges that he may have to eat his words, framed as self-directed mockery.
jokes.explanation: Ron talking to himself in the third person while using 'crow' (eating crow) is a funny character moment. His reluctant acknowledgment that Leslie might be right is delivered with Ron's characteristic stoicism. The 'Mr. Swanson' formality is very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I planned the perfect surprise party! The decorations are amazing, the food is catered by the best restaurant in town, the DJ is playing all the right songs, and—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, where's Tom?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean where's Tom? He's... he's...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Did you invite him?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I... I was so focused on making everything perfect that I forgot to actually invite him.

jokes.text: Crow for dinner tonight, Mr. Swanson?
jokes.setup: Leslie claimed she could handle everything and not fall through cracks; Ron noted she forgot to file the maintenance report. Now she's visibly doing both jobs at once.
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'Crow for dinner tonight, Mr. Swanson?' is a witty literary callback — he's asking Ron if he'll be eating crow (admitting he was wrong) about Leslie's capability. Delivered to Ron specifically.
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp, economical line. Ben's use of 'Mr. Swanson' adds formality that heightens the teasing. The idiom 'eating crow' is well-deployed and character-appropriate for the precise, literary-minded Ben. Strong economy — maximum wit per word.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can multitask. I'm doing it right now. I'm listening to you, and I'm also mentally preparing my acceptance speech for when I'm named Indiana's first female governor.

jokes.text: Leslie forgot to invite Jerry to his own surprise birthday party.
jokes.setup: The party is fully prepared — music ready, slideshow prepped — and Leslie asks April when Jerry arrives.
jokes.punchline: It dawns on the group that nobody invited Jerry. Leslie is the one who was supposed to do it. This is the same person arguing she has everything under control.
jokes.explanation: The perfect structural payoff: Leslie has spent the episode arguing she's on top of everything, and the reveal that she forgot to invite the guest of honor to his own surprise party is a devastating, well-earned punchline. The structure is near-flawless — the setup is built across the entire first act.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So these sheets are 1000 thread count?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes, that's the minimum for quality sheets.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And you're telling me these are the cheapest sheets you could find?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, I... yes. These are literally the cheapest sheets at Target.

jokes.text: I have a prediction, Ron: by the end of the night, you're going to take a bite of Jerry's cake — which incidentally we need to pick up on the way home — and say 'Sabbatical, schmabbatical. Leslie can do it all. She's the best, and I'm stupid.'
jokes.setup: Ron again tells Leslie to take a sabbatical after she forgot to invite Jerry.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's invented future quote for Ron includes 'I'm stupid' — imagining Ron saying something he would categorically never say — made funnier by the parenthetical about needing to pick up the cake.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's confabulation of what Ron will say is extremely Leslie — she invents a future where she wins and Ron capitulates completely, even calling himself stupid. The aside about needing to pick up the cake (revealing another thing she forgot) while making this triumphant declaration is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you don't have a smartphone, you don't use email, you refuse to go on social media... You're a monster.

jokes.text: That does sound like me.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just imagined Ron saying 'Sabbatical, schmabbatical. Leslie can do it all. She's the best, and I'm stupid.'
jokes.punchline: Ron's deadpan confirmation that this sounds exactly like something he'd say — which it absolutely does not.
jokes.explanation: Four words that get a huge laugh. Ron's willingness to ironically confirm Leslie's absurd invention — delivered with complete deadpan — is perfect. The joke works because the audience knows 'I'm stupid' is the most un-Ron sentence imaginable, yet he agrees it 'sounds like him.' Peak Ron economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: She likes to go hiking, I like to stay indoors and online shop for women's boots. She's a morning person, I'm a night owl. She wants to have kids, I want to have more pairs of women's boots than my girlfriend.

jokes.text: Let's talk minimum acceptable thread count for sheets. Stop me when I hit it. 1,000... 800... 700... 600? Ann, I'm at 600. Are you really not stopping me?
jokes.setup: Tom frames a relationship interrogation as 'a fun game.'
jokes.punchline: Ann's failure to stop him at any thread count — all the way down to 600 — reveals she uses cotton t-shirt sheets, which Tom cannot compute.
jokes.explanation: The descending thread-count game is very Tom — he's manufactured an entire compatibility test around luxury goods. The comedic escalation of his disbelief as the numbers drop is well-paced. 'Cotton t-shirt sheets' as the final reveal is a perfect punchline — Ann is at the absolute opposite end of Tom's spectrum.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom and Ann are fighting again. Something about his restaurant idea and her job. I don't know. I stopped listening after 'We need to talk.' That's when I discovered this bottle of wine behind my desk that I don't remember buying. Best discovery since I found out how to block people on Facebook.

jokes.text: It's always the most beautiful ladies who hurt you the worst. / She's never seen a single Paul Walker movie? That's a huge 'oh-no-no.' She also 'doesn't care' about Blu-ray? She's a monster.
jokes.setup: Tom continues cataloging Ann's failures against his standards.
jokes.punchline: Paul Walker movies and Blu-ray format preference as legitimate relationship dealbreakers, delivered with total sincerity; Ben calling Ann a 'monster' for the Blu-ray comment.
jokes.explanation: Tom's escalating dealbreakers are funny because of their absurdity (Paul Walker, Blu-ray), but the real bonus is Ben — the normally sensible character — also calling Ann a 'monster' for not caring about Blu-ray. Ben's defection to Tom's absurd value system is the extra comedic layer.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Leslie, Ron, come in here!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, what's going on?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Gail, we're coming in.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm in here! In the bathroom!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What in...

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? What's the problem? I'm just taking a bath.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, we can see you. You're... you're completely naked.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well yes, Leslie, that's how one takes a bath.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why did you call us in here?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I didn't call you in here. You called me and said you were coming over. So I was getting ready.

jokes.text: I own more pairs of Uggs than she does.
jokes.setup: Tom is listing incompatibilities with Ann.
jokes.punchline: He reveals he owns more Ugg boots than his girlfriend — a detail that functions both as a joke about Tom's fashion consumption and as a surprising gender-norm inversion.
jokes.explanation: Six words that land a solid laugh. The specificity of Uggs (associated with female fashion in this era) and Tom owning more than Ann is a perfect character detail. Very economic.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Did you lose a senior in the woods again?

jokes.text: I was getting kind of sick of listening to Tom and Ann talk about their relationship, but then I remembered that alcohol existed. Thank you, alcohol.
jokes.setup: April has been involuntarily drawn into Tom and Ann's relationship drama.
jokes.punchline: Her solution — remembering alcohol exists and thanking it — is delivered as a genuine gratitude moment.
jokes.explanation: 'Thank you, alcohol' as a sincere toast is a very April beat. The confession-to-camera format makes it land — she's sharing her genuine coping mechanism with the audience, without any embarrassment. Economical and character-true.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He's a good boy. He knows to stay close.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: See? Total obedience. Champion, come!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Champion? Champion!

jokes.text: Maybe someone else had a surprise party and actually remembered to invite him.
jokes.setup: The group can't find Jerry to bring him to his own surprise party.
jokes.punchline: Leslie bitterly notes that maybe someone threw Jerry a party and remembered the most basic step, which she failed to do.
jokes.explanation: A solid self-deprecating joke from Leslie as she acknowledges the absurdity of her failure. Functional and in-character, if not extraordinary.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So the sign company just printed whatever was in the email without checking it.

dialogue.speaker: Walter
dialogue.line: Let me read this back to you: W-W-W dot parks and rec dot gov slash events slash harvest festival underscore two thousand twelve.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, that's the website—

dialogue.speaker: Walter
dialogue.line: Hold on. There's more. Backslash admin backslash uploads backslash documents backslash.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Walter, you don't need to read every single—

dialogue.speaker: Walter
dialogue.line: I'm almost done. P-D-F question mark session equals one-seven-three-four-five-six.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ron show up in Jerry's bathroom while he's in the tub — Leslie claims it's a 'Parks emergency.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron go to Jerry's house to get him for the party.
jokes.punchline: They end up in his bathroom while he's bathing, and Leslie's cover story is an emergency that only Jerry can solve.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of finding Jerry in the bathtub — and Ron's presumably mortified presence — is good cringe. Leslie's bureaucratic framing of a 'Parks emergency' while standing in someone's bathroom is nicely absurd. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, you can't just modify your car like this. It's ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ridiculous? Ann, I've added racing stripes, a spoiler, and underglow lighting. I'm basically Ryan Gosling now.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ryan Gosling doesn't drive around with a neon sign that says 'Treat Yo' Self' on the back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's because he hasn't thought of it yet. When he does, he'll wish he was me.

jokes.text: Yes, Leslie, what ARE we doing in Jerry's bathroom?
jokes.setup: Leslie claims there's a Parks emergency requiring Jerry to leave his bath immediately.
jokes.punchline: Ron turns Leslie's question back on her with incredulous deadpan — acknowledging the absurdity of their situation.
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan agreement with the absurdity is perfectly him. He doesn't escalate or explain — he simply mirrors the question back with a slightly raised eyebrow of implied judgment. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're always trying to get out of work, you're constantly making everything about money, and you never listen to what anyone else is saying.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thank you. I've been working on those things.

jokes.text: Oh, did we lose more seniors in the woods? / No, it's a sinkhole, right?
jokes.setup: Jerry is told there's a Parks emergency requiring his immediate attention.
jokes.punchline: Jerry immediately guesses 'lost seniors in the woods' as a routine occurrence — suggesting this has happened before. Ron guesses 'sinkhole' — equally random.
jokes.explanation: The implication that 'seniors lost in the woods' is a recognizable Parks department emergency is a lovely world-building joke. The casual way both Jerry and Ron suggest municipal disasters as cover stories is very specific and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: They forgot my medication.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Jerry, you should have anticipated being kidnapped from your bath and planned accordingly.

jokes.text: Crap on a catapult. They screwed up my campaign signs.
jokes.setup: Leslie is dealing with the Jerry extraction when her phone rings.
jokes.punchline: Her expletive substitute — 'crap on a catapult' — is a Leslie-specific profanity euphemism that sounds like she's making up nonsense under pressure.
jokes.explanation: 'Crap on a catapult' is a very Leslie exclamation — alliterative, slightly absurd, family-friendly but frustrated. It's the kind of invented curse that could only be said by Leslie. Good quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Surprise!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh no, where is everyone? It's midnight.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: And Champion's gone. He ran away.

jokes.text: It's like I'm dating some idiotic game show host. He is driving me crazy with these stupid questions.
jokes.setup: Ann is venting about Tom's compatibility interrogations.
jokes.punchline: Her comparison of Tom to an 'idiotic game show host' is accurate and funny — the thread-count game, the oh-no-nos, etc.
jokes.explanation: A solid observational joke — Tom genuinely does behave like a game show host — but it doesn't add much beyond what the audience has already seen. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Champion! Come back, boy! Champion, champion, champion... you're the best dog in the... in the... *voice cracks* ...I don't know what rhymes with champion.

jokes.text: Wait, is he gonna break up with me? / ... / No, no, no, no, no, no. No. That's not how this ends, okay? I break up with him.
jokes.setup: Ann learns Tom may be thinking of ending the relationship.
jokes.punchline: Ann's immediate ego-driven pivot: not upset that it might end, but indignant that HE would break up with HER.
jokes.explanation: The gender-flipped 'I break up with him' pride beat is a reliable comedic structure that works here because Ann's vanity is underplayed enough to make it feel fresh. Her series of 'no, no, no's building to the prideful declaration is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Champion came to my voice?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, I've been using this dog whistle the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A dog whistle? Chris!

jokes.text: The campaign sign misprint: the entire URL of the image file is printed on the sign instead of Leslie's face.
jokes.setup: Leslie's campaign signs have arrived but something is wrong with them.
jokes.punchline: The printer printed the full file URL path (including 'jpeg') instead of the actual image — a long string of technical gibberish on a political campaign sign.
jokes.explanation: A great visual gag — the URL replacing the poster image is a very specific, very plausible tech-era mistake. The printer's literal-minded defense ('whatever's on the order form I print') makes it funnier. Good absurdist logic applied to a real-world frustration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, you've been such a good friend to me over the years. And tonight, I want to celebrate you by talking about something that's really important to me: my relationship with Lucy. We've decided on a couple name. We're going to be Tomcy. It's Tom and Lucy combined. Tomcy.

jokes.text: Using basic logic and human intelligence, one can surmise that this is a link to an image.
jokes.setup: Walter insists he printed exactly what was on the order form.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's extremely patient, slightly condescending explanation that a URL is not meant to be printed.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's 'basic logic and human intelligence' framing is a small but nice touch — she's genuinely restraining herself. Functional joke in the URL sequence, not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've been working on our couple name. Are you ready? Tann. T-Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's the worst thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: That's a good sign. You should've used that.
jokes.setup: Leslie shows the printer what the sign SHOULD have looked like.
jokes.punchline: Walter simply admires it and suggests she should have used that — as if this is helpful new information rather than salt in the wound.
jokes.explanation: Perfect oblivious deadpan. Walter's suggestion that Leslie 'should've used that' sign — after she already did everything wrong and explained it all — is the ideal button to this sequence. Maximum funny per word; the obliviousness is total and genuine.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'd like to propose a toast. First of all, no shoes on the furniture. Second, all dishes must be washed immediately after use. Third, quiet hours are from 10 PM to 8 AM. Fourth, if you're going to use the last of the milk, you replace it. And finally, under no circumstances are you to touch my things in the refrigerator.

jokes.text: That's highly against protocol. / [Leslie shows Walter the actual design.] / 'That's a good sign. You should've used that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie shows Walter what the sign was supposed to look like.
jokes.punchline: Walter objects to being shown the design ('highly against protocol') but immediately declares it a good sign and says she should've used it — without acknowledging his role in not using it.
jokes.explanation: 'That's a good sign. You should've used that.' is a perfectly calibrated Walter button — he genuinely admires the design while completely deflecting any responsibility. The 'highly against protocol' resistance followed by immediate aesthetic opinion is a great two-beat structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Jerry, you're a good man. And I say that with the utmost sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You show up to work every day, you do your job, and you don't complain. Well, you do complain, but not as much as you could.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: So, Jerry... you're not the worst.

jokes.text: You told April you were breaking up with me? / Ann, we consistently disagree on 'who wore it best.' You still use an iPad one. You read books all the time.
jokes.setup: Ann confronts Tom about his rumored breakup plans.
jokes.punchline: Tom's list of Ann's disqualifying traits: 'who wore it best' disagreements, using an iPad 1, and reading books — delivered as if these are serious character flaws.
jokes.explanation: iPad 1 and reading books as relationship dealbreakers is very Tom. 'You read books all the time' — delivered as an indictment — is the funniest of the three. Good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have so much to be thankful for. My health, my friends, my family. But I'm also grateful for some of the smaller things in life. Like the fact that I can touch my nose with my tongue. And that I've never broken a bone. And that I can name all the US state capitals in alphabetical order.

jokes.text: You put 20-inch rims on your Volkswagen Golf, and you insist on being introduced as 'the brown Gosling.'
jokes.setup: Ann fires back with her own list of Tom's dealbreaking qualities.
jokes.punchline: Tom calling himself 'the brown Gosling' (i.e., Ryan Gosling) is a perfect Tom ego detail. The Volkswagen Golf with 20-inch rims is also exactly the kind of try-hard move Tom would make.
jokes.explanation: 'The brown Gosling' is one of the best Tom lines in the episode. It's perfectly him — grandiose, race-conscious in a self-congratulatory way, and genuinely funny as a self-appointed nickname. The Volkswagen Golf with 20-inch rims adds to the portrait of someone who tries very hard in exactly the wrong ways. This is 'could only be Tom' writing at its best. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh no, oh no, oh no. April's asleep on me. If I move, she'll wake up. If I don't move, I'll be stuck here for hours.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Just enjoy the moment, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Easy for you to say! You're not the one slowly losing feeling in your arm!

jokes.text: Everything you just said makes me like me more.
jokes.setup: Ann has just listed Tom's most embarrassing qualities as dealbreakers.
jokes.punchline: Tom's response reveals he has no self-awareness — or too much self-love — and Ann's criticisms land as compliments.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect single-line character joke. Tom's unassailable self-regard — where criticism can only make him like himself more — is the core of his character, distilled into eight words. It's not just that he disagrees; he's genuinely energized by her criticism. The economy is exceptional. One of the episode's best individual lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a dream of working with cow leather before and after it was on the cow.

jokes.text: I can't take it anymore, okay? I'm breaking you up. You guys are done.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ann are arguing about breaking up.
jokes.punchline: April — drunk — unilaterally declares the relationship over as if she has authority over it.
jokes.explanation: April exercising nonexistent authority to end the relationship — while drunk — is a great beat. Her exhaustion with the situation translating into a unilateral decree is very April. The 'You guys are done' delivery (one imagines) is magnificently flat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I had three jobs by the time I was in middle school. I was working at a sawmill, I had a small firearms manufacturing operation in my garage, and I was doing carpentry on the side.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's incredible. How old were you?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Eleven.

jokes.text: Fine with me. / Fine, fine. / Oh, April. / I'm drunk. You made me drunk, you made me drunk, and you--
jokes.setup: April has just broken up Tom and Ann.
jokes.punchline: Both Tom and Ann immediately agree to the breakup ('Fine with me' / 'Fine, fine'), then April — who wanted this — drunkenly assigns blame.
jokes.explanation: The speed of Tom and Ann's mutual 'fine' — suggesting neither was that invested — followed by April's drunken blame cascade is a nicely structured beat. The humor of April blaming them for making her drunk enough to get involved is good character comedy.

jokes.text: Why are you guys even fighting anyway? It's so stupid. 'I hate Ann because of this stupid reason.' 'And I hate Tom for this stupid reason.' Who cares?
jokes.setup: April is drunk and being carried to bed by Tom and Ann.
jokes.punchline: April delivers relationship wisdom in her most dismissive possible voice — summarizing both Tom and Ann's grievances as '[stupid reason]' — which is both accurate and completely unhelpful.
jokes.explanation: April's drunk relationship advice — summarizing both positions as 'stupid reason' — is perfectly in character: she's right but also completely checked out. The meta-placeholder of '[stupid reason]' for actual grievances is funny and works as commentary on the whole subplot.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I hate them.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know. And that's what makes you so great.

jokes.text: Well, we didn't get to the drug store for my liver medication. / Well, you should've thought about that before we dragged you out of the bath, Jerry.
jokes.setup: Leslie is listing everything they accomplished despite the chaos.
jokes.punchline: Jerry reveals they missed getting his liver medication; Ron has zero sympathy — placing the blame on Jerry for being in the bath.
jokes.explanation: Ron's completely logic-free victim-blaming of Jerry for not getting his liver medication — because Jerry was in the bath they intruded upon — is dark and funny. The implication that Jerry's liver is at stake makes it extra. Very Ron to frame this as Jerry's fault.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Wait, are you sending me to Muncie?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How did you... I mean, yes. How did you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Lucky guess.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am genuinely shocked that you correctly identified the least glamorous destination in Indiana on your first try.

jokes.text: Surprise! / Oh, what the [bleep]?
jokes.setup: Jerry is finally brought to the house for his surprise party.
jokes.punchline: Jerry's extremely unexpected and profane reaction to his own surprise party.
jokes.explanation: Jerry's profane surprise reaction is funny because Jerry is mild-mannered — the bleep implies something genuinely strong. It's also the payoff to the entire party-planning chaos. The contrast between the effort to get him there and his instinctive response lands well.

jokes.text: Where the hell is everybody? / Well, it got so late. We just weren't sure you were still coming. Everybody's either in bed or out looking for Champion.
jokes.setup: Jerry arrives at his surprise party, which has dissolved due to the chaos of the evening.
jokes.punchline: The party has essentially dispersed — half the guests are asleep, the other half are searching for a lost three-legged dog — leaving Jerry's birthday to an empty room.
jokes.explanation: The compounding of all the episode's B-plots — Champion running away, people going to bed — resulting in an empty party for Jerry is well-constructed situational comedy. It's Jerry's cosmic unluckiness playing out again.

jokes.text: We are gonna throw Jerry an amazing Sweet 16 surprise party no matter how agonizing it is for all of us.
jokes.setup: The surprise party has mostly collapsed.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's rallying cry accidentally includes 'no matter how agonizing it is for all of us' — framing Jerry's party as a trial.
jokes.explanation: The unintentional honesty in Leslie's pep talk — 'no matter how agonizing it is for all of us' — reveals the actual emotional experience of the night. She's too committed to notice the backhanded quality of her speech. Very Leslie.

jokes.text: I have an organic, gluten-free soy bone for you.
jokes.setup: Chris is calling out for Champion in the woods.
jokes.punchline: His dog treat is organic, gluten-free, and soy — the height of Chris's health optimization applied to dog food.
jokes.explanation: Chris's obsessive health consciousness extended to dog treats is a perfect character detail. 'Organic, gluten-free soy bone' is a funny specific because it reveals he's applied his nutrition philosophy to a dog. Short and well-integrated.

jokes.text: Yeah, it was really good. I was gonna give it to Champion, but it just — it looked so yummy.
jokes.setup: Chris mentions a soy bone he brought for Champion.
jokes.punchline: Andy has already eaten it — a dog treat — and found it genuinely delicious.
jokes.explanation: Andy eating a dog treat is very Andy — he has the dietary discrimination of a toddler. 'It just looked so yummy' delivered with genuine enthusiasm is excellent. The confession-to-Chris setup and Andy's complete lack of shame makes it land. High character integration.

jokes.text: I feel naked without it, okay.
jokes.setup: Chris asks Andy to sing to Champion to lure him back; Andy protests he doesn't have his guitar.
jokes.punchline: Andy describes his relationship with his guitar as a matter of felt nudity — sincere and slightly more intimate than expected.
jokes.explanation: A minor but sweet Andy line. His emotional attachment to his guitar framed as nudity is endearing and mildly funny. Not a big laugh but character-consistent.

jokes.text: Andy improvises a song to call Champion back: '### Champion, you're lost / and soon you'll be found / I rescued you from the pound, / something something / oh man / on the ground / get on out of here ###'
jokes.setup: Chris suggests Andy sing to Champion because the dog responds to his music.
jokes.punchline: Andy's song is heartfelt but completely falls apart mid-lyric with 'something something / oh man' — then Champion returns anyway.
jokes.explanation: The song is perfectly Andy — genuine emotion, terrible craft. 'Something something / oh man' as visible lyric failure in real time is an inspired choice. The fact that Champion comes back ANYWAY (to this mess of a song) makes it even funnier and sweeter. High character integration; only Andy would sing this song and only Champion would respond to it.

jokes.text: Dog whistle.
jokes.setup: Champion returns to Andy after his terrible improvised song; Andy is moved, believing Champion responded to his voice.
jokes.punchline: Chris reveals he used a dog whistle — immediately deflating the emotional moment.
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect structure: emotional buildup (Andy's touching reunion belief) → instant deflation. 'Dog whistle' is delivered with complete Chris positivity — he's not trying to undercut Andy, he just wants to be helpful. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny, it's character-true (of course Chris has a dog whistle), and the timing is perfect. One of the episode's best constructed jokes for its economy.

jokes.text: Dog whistle. [April holds up a dog whistle after Champion returns to Andy's singing]
jokes.setup: Champion miraculously returns to Andy's improvised singing, creating an emotional moment about the power of love and music.
jokes.punchline: April reveals she blew a dog whistle — immediately deflating the heartwarming moment with practical reality.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum comedic and emotional impact. April's 'dog whistle' reveal is expertly structured misdirection: the show builds a genuine emotional beat (Andy's love reaches his dog through song), and April instantly punctures it with mundane reality. This is precisely April's character — she creates the heartwarming moment but won't admit it. The economy is perfect (10/10), the character integration is maximal, and the structure is a textbook misdirection payoff. This is the episode's single best joke — it does multiple things simultaneously and the two-word delivery would get a massive reaction from a room. Earns 8.7 craft because the setup was built over multiple scenes, the deflation is perfectly timed, and it reveals April's hidden affection under the cynicism.

jokes.text: Why is your arm around her? I broke you up.
jokes.setup: April wakes up to find Tom and Ann have reconciled.
jokes.punchline: April's first waking words assert her authority over their breakup — she's still invested despite claiming not to care.
jokes.explanation: April's immediate claim of authority over the relationship — contradicting her stated indifference — is the payoff to her earlier 'I don't care about anyone' confessional. The contrast between professed nihilism and actual investment is a lovely character note.

jokes.text: Yeah, when we were carrying you to bed, you correctly pointed out that we were arguing about stuff that was stupid. / I'm drunk. Don't listen to me, no.
jokes.setup: Tom explains that April's drunk advice led to their reconciliation.
jokes.punchline: April frantically tries to retroactively revoke her wisdom — she doesn't want credit for good advice.
jokes.explanation: April's horror at accidentally being responsible for good relationship advice is excellent character comedy. Her desperately offering 'I'm drunk, don't listen to me' as a disclaimer is the right line. The joke works because it confirms her actual investment despite her nihilist pose.

jokes.text: Okay, I want everyone to go around and tell their favorite Jerry story. / A positive one.
jokes.setup: Leslie initiates a round of Jerry appreciation at his party.
jokes.punchline: The immediate qualifier 'A positive one' implies that non-positive Jerry stories are so numerous and readily available that she had to specifically rule them out.
jokes.explanation: The pause and then 'A positive one' is perfectly timed and perfectly Leslie. It reveals so much in three words: the default mode for Jerry stories is negative, and the group needed to be explicitly steered away from that. The economy is excellent — the qualifier alone contains the entire joke.

jokes.text: Jerry, today is your birthday, but it's about much more than that. It's also about Ann and I getting back together and being the hottest couple in Pawnee. I'd also like to announce our official relationship mash-up name. It's 'Tan.' To Tan.
jokes.setup: Tom is asked to share a positive Jerry story at Jerry's birthday party.
jokes.punchline: Tom uses Jerry's birthday speech moment to announce his own relationship news and toast himself.
jokes.explanation: Tom hijacking Jerry's birthday party speech to announce his own relationship revival — and toasting himself as 'the hottest couple in Pawnee' — is peak Tom Haverford. The celebrity mash-up name 'Tan' (Tom + Ann) delivered with total sincerity is also excellent. This is character comedy at its most concentrated. The contrast with what the moment was supposed to be (positive Jerry stories) makes it even funnier.

jokes.text: I would like to announce that the name Tan is officially over. / To the end of Tan.
jokes.setup: Tom has just proposed the couple name 'Tan.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately shuts it down and toasts its end — the group drinks to the death of 'Tan.'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's speed and authority in killing 'Tan' — and the group cheerfully drinking to its death — is a great beat. The reversal of the toast (to ending something rather than celebrating it) is a nice structural inversion.

jokes.text: I would like to address the fact that rule number seven says 'no pets,' and yet there is a three-legged animal in my living room.
jokes.setup: The party is underway; Champion has been found and brought inside.
jokes.punchline: Donna's contribution to the positive-Jerry-story round is to raise a house rule violation — with 'three-legged animal' rather than 'dog.'
jokes.explanation: Donna's legalistic address of the pet violation — and her use of 'three-legged animal' rather than 'dog' — is a strong Donna moment. She's not even acknowledging the birthday speech context, just raising a concern. Very character-true.

jokes.text: Jerry's work is often adequate.
jokes.setup: The group is sharing positive Jerry stories. Ron is up.
jokes.punchline: Ron's highest available praise for Jerry is 'often adequate' — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is generous.
jokes.explanation: The best single line in the episode. Ron's damning-with-faint-praise — 'often adequate' — is delivered as a sincere compliment, which makes it devastating. 'Often' does enormous work here; it's not even consistently adequate. The four words (following Leslie's long earnest setup) land like a perfect deadpan bomb. Economy: 10/10. Character integration: 10/10. This is the kind of line that defines a character.

jokes.text: Ron's pause after 'Jerry's work is often adequate' — he nods slightly, as if he's said everything that needed to be said.
jokes.setup: Ron has delivered his positive Jerry story.
jokes.punchline: The implied satisfied pause — Ron clearly believes he's been generous — is the button to the line.
jokes.explanation: The silent beat after Ron's faint praise is integral to the joke — it's Ron's self-satisfaction in the pause that completes it. His belief that he's contributed meaningfully to a positive birthday tribute is what makes the deadpan work.

jokes.text: Jerry, I'll go. Jerry has a wife and three beautiful daughters — a full life — and that's amazing. April and Andy have Champion, and that's amazing. I have a stepbrother who lives in London and 2.8% body fat.
jokes.setup: Chris gives his positive Jerry story at the birthday.
jokes.punchline: After genuinely touching observations about Jerry's family and Andy/April's dog, Chris pivots to listing his own assets — a stepbrother in London and 2.8% body fat — as if these are equivalent relationship goods.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed bit: Chris starts genuinely warm about Jerry and Andy/April, then the structure pivots to self-inventory — revealing his loneliness through the accumulation. '2.8% body fat' as a listed life possession is both a great Chris joke and a melancholy window into his character. The juxtaposition of 'wife, three daughters, full life' with 'stepbrother in London and 2.8% body fat' lands the joke and the pathos simultaneously. One of the episode's better crafted moments.

jokes.text: Guys... guys... What do I do? I mean, she's asleep. / You probably should just sit there and not move. She's really tired. Just a few hours.
jokes.setup: April has fallen asleep on Ben and he's trapped under her.
jokes.punchline: Tom and Ann's helpful advice: sit there for a few hours and don't move.
jokes.explanation: A mild physical comedy situation. The image of Ben trapped under a sleeping April is funny but the joke doesn't develop much. Tom and Ann's advice is basic. Functional.

jokes.text: Is this all the eggs we have? / Yes. / What are you making? / Eggs.
jokes.setup: Morning after the party; Ron is in the kitchen.
jokes.punchline: Ron's answer to 'what are you making' is simply 'eggs' — tautological, but delivered with Ron's characteristic self-evidence.
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'Eggs' in response to 'what are you making' — after being asked if those are all the eggs — is a small but Ron-perfect tautology. He doesn't elaborate because it's self-evident. Brief and character-true.

jokes.text: Surprise! / Oh, God. What happened? / Well, you slept with Jerry last night.
jokes.setup: Leslie pops out for a 'morning surprise party.' Jerry woke up not knowing where he was.
jokes.punchline: Leslie says 'you slept with Jerry last night' — with an obvious double meaning — before clarifying it was just Leslie's party planning.
jokes.explanation: The 'slept with Jerry' misdirection is a standard double-entendre structure — it gets a laugh but it's not particularly sophisticated. The clarification follows immediately. Competent but familiar.

jokes.text: Morning surprise parties are always the best.
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals she planned a morning surprise party for Jerry.
jokes.punchline: Leslie states as fact that morning surprise parties are 'always the best' — a category she has clearly just invented.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's confident assertion of a non-existent category as universal wisdom is peak Leslie. She says this with complete authority, as if morning surprise parties are a well-established tradition everyone knows is superior. Good character integration.

jokes.text: I used to work in a sheet metal factory, but then a job came along at the tannery. The hours were better, and I would get paid. Also I'd have the chance to work with leather both before and after it was on the cow, which had always been a dream of mine.
jokes.setup: Ron is telling a story to make a point about Leslie taking on too much.
jokes.punchline: Ron's backstory includes 'which had always been a dream of mine' about working with leather — a dream nobody asked about and entirely Ron.
jokes.explanation: Ron casually disclosing that working with leather 'both before and after it was on the cow' was a childhood dream is deeply funny — it's so specific and so Ron. The 'before and after it was on the cow' construction is also inherently funny as a description. High character integration.

jokes.text: I was so tired, I tried to puncture an eight-gauge aluminum foil with a leather awl.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining the consequences of overextending himself across two jobs.
jokes.punchline: His example of fatigue-induced incompetence is highly technical and specific — 'eight-gauge aluminum foil' and 'leather awl' suggests someone who knows exactly what he's doing, yet was so tired he confused the tools.
jokes.explanation: The extreme technical specificity of Ron's error — the wrong gauge, the wrong tool — is funnier than a vague 'I made mistakes.' Only Ron would frame his worst moment this precisely. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Never half-ass two things. Whole-ass one thing.
jokes.setup: Ron has told his two-jobs story and is delivering the moral.
jokes.punchline: The aphorism inverts the normal 'don't half-ass things' advice into 'whole-ass one thing' — Ron-ifying a piece of wisdom with his characteristic bluntness.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of Parks and Recreation's most iconic lines. 'Whole-ass one thing' is the perfect linguistic construction — it takes the vulgarity of 'half-ass' and inverts it into a positive, creating a memorable aphorism that's also a great Ron Swanson character moment. The structure is flawless: 'never half-ass two things' sets the expected framework, 'whole-ass one thing' lands the subversion. Economy is perfect. This is a quote that escaped the show and entered common usage. Comparable in quality and impact to the anchor example of 'never go with a hippie to a second location.'

jokes.text: Deal. / 15. / 10. / Deal.
jokes.setup: Ron tells Leslie to take a sabbatical; Leslie counter-offers 10 hours a week. Ron says 15. Leslie says 10 again.
jokes.punchline: Ron accepts 10 hours — the same number Leslie originally proposed — after briefly holding out for 15.
jokes.explanation: The rapid negotiation — Ron folds immediately at his own counter — is funny as a character beat. Leslie wins the negotiation through sheer stubbornness without even trying. Good economy in the exchange.

jokes.text: Ugh, I can't believe I got them back together. Now they're always gonna want to come talk to me about stuff.
jokes.setup: April has accidentally been the catalyst for Tom and Ann's reconciliation.
jokes.punchline: Her complaint is not that she helped — but that she'll now be expected to help again.
jokes.explanation: A good callback to April's earlier nihilism — now she's paying the price for having accidentally done something kind. Her horror at the prospect of future emotional involvement is very April.

jokes.text: They want to talk to you because you're important to them. / Yes, but I hate them. / I know you do, sweetheart.
jokes.setup: Andy tries to reframe April's importance to Tom and Ann as a positive.
jokes.punchline: April says she hates them; Andy accepts this with complete warmth — 'I know you do, sweetheart' — treating 'I hate them' as a normal thing to say.
jokes.explanation: 'I know you do, sweetheart' is an exceptional line — Andy accepting April's professed hatred of their friends as a perfectly reasonable statement he can accommodate. The warmth of 'sweetheart' combined with the complete validation of 'I hate them' captures their relationship perfectly. High character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: Oh, hey, I told Chris he can borrow Champion whenever. / Andy, he's kissing me.
jokes.setup: Andy mentions he's arranged for Chris to borrow Champion.
jokes.punchline: April reveals Champion has immediately made himself at home on her face — Chris's influence already taking hold.
jokes.explanation: A sweet visual button — Champion kissing April, who is simultaneously complaining about having people come talk to her, is a nice ironic contrast. April being kissed by the dog she just helped rescue is gently warm.

jokes.text: We are sending you and Gayle to a B&B in your favorite place in the world. / Muncie? / Amazingly, yes. Muncie, Indiana.
jokes.setup: The group presents Jerry with a birthday gift — a B&B trip to his favorite place.
jokes.punchline: Jerry's favorite place in the world is Muncie, Indiana — a deeply ordinary Midwest city. 'Amazingly, yes' from Leslie confirms that she too cannot believe this is true.
jokes.explanation: Muncie, Indiana as Jerry's dream destination is a perfect Jerry detail — modest, sincere, and slightly heartbreaking. 'Amazingly, yes' is the ideal Leslie reaction: she can't believe it's true but she's committed to honoring it. Good character integration for both.

jokes.text: Thank you, guys. It was really expensive. / Oh, campaign. / Take it.
jokes.setup: Jerry thanks them for the expensive gift.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reaction — 'campaign' — reveals she just realized she spent campaign funds on Jerry's birthday; Ben tells her to let it go.
jokes.explanation: The quick exchange — Leslie's horrified single-word 'campaign,' Ben's 'Take it' — is economical and character-true. The irony that Leslie, who has been struggling to keep campaign and work separate, spent campaign money on a work birthday party is a nice structural callback to the episode's premise.

tmdb_overview: Leslie realizes that the department has forgotten Jerry's birthday and decides to throw a party for him at a special location. Meanwhile, Tom is flabbergasted when he finds out Ann doesn't share his taste in music.
insight: Steady character work drives a mid-tier ep; 58 jokes land despite modest 75.6 score.
